title: Year five opens: reading for yourself
hookLine: a quote card with a saint's name under it: did he ever actually write that?
tomorrow: so what are the first words Augustine actually wrote?

lines: A SAINT'S NAME UNDER A SUNSET.
cards: A quote card slides past in your feed: a sunset, a line in soft script, and a saint's name underneath. The hearts pile up. Nobody in the comments asks where he wrote it, or what came before it, or after.

The line might be his. It might be a summary of a summary, polished until it sounds like a saint. So, one question for the year: why read the old voices yourself, when a summary is always one tap away?

teach.b: Historians have a name for the real thing: a primary source. A letter, a diary, a confession, written by the person who was there. A book about it is a secondary source.
Both help. Only one lets you hear the person.

teach.h: WE HAVE SEEN WITH OUR EYES.
teach.b: The first letter of John opens like a witness taking the stand, in the Douay-Rheims: "which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled." Not a rumor. We were there.
That's the Catholic answer to the question: summaries tell you about someone; their own words let you meet them. So this year, the saints talk.
First Augustine's Confessions, then The Imitation of Christ, Francis de Sales and Thérèse of Lisieux, each in an older English translation anyone may read.
One honest caution: a translation is a window, not the voice itself. Augustine wrote in Latin, so you'll hear him through a translator, thou and thee and all. A window still lets the light in.
Muslim neighbors know this question from the inside.

teach.h: READ: IN THE NAME OF THY LORD.
teach.b: Tradition says the first words revealed to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, began with one command, in Pickthall's 1930 English: "Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth."
Shared ground: both traditions treat reading as more than gathering facts; you go to the words themselves. And one honest difference.
For Muslims, the Qur'an's Arabic is God's own speech, so Pickthall called his English book The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, not the Koran.
Augustine's Latin is a saint's human voice, reaching for God, and the saints' books aren't Scripture for Catholics at all.
In the Office of Readings, Catholics hear a saint's page set beside the Scripture reading: a family still listening to its own.

how: Catholics meet the saints' own writings in the Office of Readings of the Liturgy of the Hours, which sets a passage from a saint or a Father of the Church beside a Scripture reading, and in slow spiritual reading at home.

games.q: a clip online builds a whole argument on "a saint once said…" and it's being shared everywhere. what do you do first?
o: find the saint's own text and read the lines around that sentence.
trust it: the person in the clip clearly knows a lot about saints.
check which version of the quote has the most shares.
games.why: a primary source lets you meet the person, not someone's version of them. how many people shared it, or who said it, isn't the same as where it's written.

practice: If there's an old book within reach, a Bible, a saint's writings, anything good and old, open it to the first page and say the first few lines out loud, slowly, the way a letter is read at a table.
If there isn't, say the opening of a prayer or text you know by heart, the writer's words, not a summary of them. Then rest in what you heard.

wordCard.voice: Primary source. A text in the writer's own words, from someone who was there, not a book about them.

carryVoice: Your line: in their own words. A translator's window, and a saint's voice on the other side. Year five, day one.
